s: Today we're talking about character — the inner qualities that help people handle hard times, win others over, and stay true to themselves.
We picked seven strong words for you: resilient, vulnerable, charisma, perseverance, composure, restless, and integrity.
Big words, but don't worry — by the end of this episode, you'll use them naturally.
And we have real stories to make them stick.
Plus, we'll say each word at least four or five times, so it really lands.
Before we dive in, a quick word about the Muse English app.

If you're enjoying this podcast, the free app takes your learning further: daily words with photos and pronunciation audio, this podcast with full transcripts, shadowing stories, quizzes, grammar lessons, and a leaderboard with points for every lesson you finish.
It's everything in one place, and it's free to install.
And that's today's app tip from Maya — I'll do the second one later in the show.
Maya, have you ever had one of those weeks where everything goes wrong at work?
Two years ago, my whole project got cancelled.
Six months of work, gone overnight.
That is exactly when you find out if you are resilient.
A resilient person doesn't bounce back in one day, but they don't stay down forever either.
They grieve, they adjust, and they start again.
I remember thinking, okay, the project died, but my skills didn't.
Within a month, I was on a better team.
And perseverance helped too, I bet.
Perseverance is continuing to try even when things are very difficult.
It's the quiet decision to keep going.
Yes — perseverance is what gets you through the boring middle part, when the excitement is gone and only discipline is left.
And there's one more thing that mattered that week: integrity.
Even though I was frustrated, I kept acting with integrity.
I finished my handover properly, I helped my colleagues, I didn't badmouth anyone.
That's integrity — being honest and having strong principles, even when nobody would know if you cut corners.
Let me tell you about my friend Daniel.
He runs marathons, and his story is pure perseverance.
Last year, he hit the wall at kilometre thirty.
The wall — when your body just says no.
He slowed down, he drank some water, he kept moving.
Perseverance isn't about speed; it's about refusing to stop.
And you know what surprised him most?
He said the training had made him more resilient in everyday life too.
Now when work gets stressful, he thinks, I ran forty-two kilometres.
That's the thing about a resilient attitude — once you build it in one area, it spreads everywhere.
And runners need composure as well.
Composure is staying calm and controlled under pressure.
At kilometre thirty-five, Daniel said his mind wanted to panic.
Instead, he focused on his breathing and kept his composure, one kilometre at a time.
Lena, you're on a hiring panel — what catches your eye?
Charisma is that special personal quality that draws people in.
You can teach skills, but charisma is harder to learn.
I once interviewed a candidate who had charisma from the moment she walked in.
She wasn't the most qualified on paper, but her charisma made everyone in the room sit up and listen.
But here's the interesting part — she told me later she felt completely vulnerable during that interview.
Vulnerable means open to being hurt, exposed, unprotected.
She had left her old job without a plan, and this interview was everything.
She turned that vulnerable feeling into honesty, and honesty is magnetic.
The panel asked her a really tough question about a gap in her resume, and she didn't panic.
She paused, smiled, and answered with total composure.
So charisma opened the door, vulnerability made her human, and composure closed the deal.
A quick reminder, everyone — the Muse English app.
This is Lena with your second app tip.

Inside the app you'll find every word from today's episode with a photo, a pronunciation guide, and audio clips, plus the full transcript of this podcast, a shadowing story to practise speaking, daily quizzes, and clear grammar lessons.
Install it free and turn your commute into an English class.
That second app tip was mine last time, Lena.
There's a side of these words that's softer.
Being vulnerable with a friend — actually saying, I'm struggling — that changes a relationship.
I used to think being vulnerable was a weakness.
Then a close friend told me she was going through a hard time, and instead of giving advice, I just said, me too.
That vulnerable honesty brought us so much closer.
When someone lets you see their vulnerable side, it says, I trust you.
And that trust is the foundation of real friendship.
A friend with integrity keeps your secrets.
They tell you the truth even when it's uncomfortable.
That's the kind of person you call at midnight.
When I know someone has my back, I recover from setbacks so much faster.
A resilient person is rarely resilient alone.
Now let's talk about leadership, because leaders live these words every day.
Imagine a captain during a storm — literally or at work.
I worked for a manager who never lost her composure, not even when a client threatened to cancel.
Her composure calmed the whole team.
When the leader is steady, everyone breathes easier.
And keeping your composure isn't about having no feelings.
She told me she was terrified inside.
Composure is choosing calm behaviour even when your heart is racing.
The best leaders also lead with integrity.
A leader with integrity admits mistakes.
Our manager once told the whole team, I got this wrong, and here's how we'll fix it.
Nobody lost respect for her — they gained it.
And then there's charisma in leadership.
Some leaders inspire just by walking into a room.
That kind of charisma comes from confidence and genuine care for people.
Right — charisma without integrity is just manipulation.
That's leadership people follow for years.
Lena, have you ever felt restless at work — like everything is fine, but something inside says, this isn't it?
Restless means unable to stay calm or still, usually because of worry, boredom, or excitement.
Two years ago I felt deeply restless in my old job.
The pay was good, the team was nice, but I was restless every single Sunday night.
Being restless isn't always bad, though.
Sometimes that restless energy is your mind telling you it's time to grow.
My restlessness pushed me to take a course, and that course led me here.
If I hadn't listened to that restless voice, I'd still be in the same chair.
A restless person who keeps jumping without a plan just gets tired.
The trick is to channel that energy.
When I started this job, everything was new and scary.
My perseverance got me through the first difficult months — showing up, learning, asking questions, refusing to quit.
And here's something people forget: changing your life means being vulnerable again.
New city, new job, new people — you feel vulnerable, like a beginner.
Feeling vulnerable in a new place just means you care.
And every time you survive it, you get more resilient.
Look at us — two formerly restless, vulnerable beginners, now hosting a podcast.
Quick listener question before we wrap.
Sara from Toronto asks: which of today's words best describes a good teammate?
I'd say a good teammate is resilient — they recover from mistakes instead of blaming others.
They also show integrity, doing the right thing even when the boss isn't watching.
A teammate with perseverance keeps pushing when the project gets hard.
And honestly, a little vulnerability helps too — saying I don't know this, can you help me, builds trust fast.
When the server crashes at midnight, you want the teammate who keeps their composure, not the one who panics.
Sara, there's your dream team: resilient, full of integrity, with real perseverance, honest vulnerability, and calm composure.
Resilient — able to recover after difficulties.
A resilient person gets back up.
Vulnerable — open to being hurt or exposed.
Charisma — the quality that attracts people.
Restless — unable to stay still, driven to change.
That restless feeling might mean growth.
And integrity — honesty and strong principles.
Which one do you want to build this week?
Pick one and practise it in the app — the shadowing story today uses all seven, so you can say them out loud.
Thanks for listening to Muse English!
